verdict.reasoning: Patient says breathlessness has been “slowly getting worse over the last couple of weeks” and “become quite troublesome the last few days,” matching progressive SOB for ~2 weeks, worse in recent days.

Patient notes he is “having to sort of sit down and catch my breath” when walking to the shops and is “even starting to get a bit breathless just about the house,” consistent with dyspnea on minimal exertion and around the house.
Transcript notes “I’ve got a bit of a dry cough, but it’s not too troublesome” but does not specify duration; “for several days” is not stated.

Patient reports “my ankles have gotten bigger… they’ve sort of swollen up a bit… both ankles,” and when asked duration says “I kind of noticed it the last few days,” supporting new bilateral ankle swelling over the past few days.
Patient denies chest pain (“No pain in my chest”), palpitations (“No, not really” to palpitations or skipped heartbeat), and fever (“No” to temperatures or fevers).

Appetite: Doctor asks “Are you eating and drinking? Okay.” Patient: “Yeah, that’s fine.” Urination: Doctor asks “Are you passing urine? Okay.” Patient: “Yeah. Yeah, I usually pee a lot,” indicating normal appetite and urination.
Patient explicitly says “Yeah. Yeah, I usually pee a lot.”
Patient states “I’ve got heart failure” and doctor later refers to “having diagnosed with heart failure.”
Patient says “I was told I had, like. They called it, like, a small heart attack about five years ago… they took me to hospital,” matching a small heart attack ~5 years ago.
Patient: “Yeah, I take something called furosemide.” When asked dose: “I can’t remember… I have to check,” so dose is unknown.
Patient lists “Yeah, I take aspirin.”
Doctor prompts “Metoprolol. Was this…” after listing medications, indicating metoprolol is among regular medications.
Patient adds “Simvastatin,” and doctor acknowledges it.
Doctor asks “Any allergies at all? Any medications?” Patient replies, “No, no allergies.”
Patient says “My father died of a heart attack.” When asked age: “He was early 60s,” consistent with MI in early 60s.
Patient: “My mother had osteoporosis.” Doctor asks “Is your mother still with us?” Patient: “Yeah, she’s still living.”
Patient says “I live on my own. I got two cats… They’re my family.”
Patient: “I work part time as a lorry driver.” Later: “Oh, no, I only take shifts during the day. I don’t like working at night,” supporting part-time day-shift lorry driving.
Patient is ex-smoker: “Not anymore” to smoking and confirms he “used to smoke… about a pack a day… for a good 25 years,” matching one pack/day for ~25 years.
Patient states “I don’t drink alcohol.”
Patient: “I try and walk to the shops least once a day.”
Doctor says “having examined you, your chest and your saturations and blood pressure, all. Okay,” indicating a chest exam was performed.
Same line: “having examined you, your chest and your saturations and blood pressure, all. Okay,” shows oxygen saturation and blood pressure were assessed and found okay.

Doctor: “I wonder whether you’ve had a flare up of your heart failure… your heart’s not pumping as well as it should be,” based on progressive breathlessness, ankle swelling, dry cough, and known heart failure with prior ‘small heart attack,’ supporting probable HF exacerbation.

History of ‘small heart attack’ and current heart failure imply underlying coronary artery disease with remote MI; doctor explores this as more than angina, supporting CAD with remote MI as a reasonable direct clinical inference.

Doctor: “rather than one tablet day, we can give you two tablets a day for the first few days” and later “increase your frusamide to one tablet twice a day,” which is doubling the prior once-daily regimen; dose strength remains unspecified.

Doctor: “let’s get a blood test done. We can check your full blood count, look for signs of anemia, we can have a check your kidney function,” matching FBC and renal function to assess anemia and kidneys.

Doctor plans “maybe an echocardiogram of your heart to see how well your heart’s pumping… It’s a jelly scan… that’s something I can organize for you today. And they may take a week or two weeks for that to be organized,” consistent with transthoracic echo in 1–2 weeks to assess LV function.
Doctor: “I really would like you to come back and see me in about a week’s time to see how you’re getting on,” i.e., review in ~1 week after increasing diuretic.

Doctor advises: “if you are getting more unwell, so if you’re getting more breathless or you’re having any other symptoms like chest pain or palpitations or dizziness, then… give me a call sooner,” matching the stated safety-net advice.
